To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The compression of the nuclear matter in central collisions of heavy ions around 50 MeV/n leads to the formation of unstable rings and bubbles; 2) the bubble and ring formation can be observed by measuring the number of fragments and the fragment Coulomb acceleration pattern; and 3) the bubble and rings are not formed by a phase transition, but rather by a dynamical effect of the nuclear transport theory.
the formation of bubbles and rings in central nuclear collisions leads to a higher number of fragments and a different fragment Coulomb acceleration pattern.

the formation of unstable bubble and ring structures around {ital E}/{it A}{approx} 50 MeV/nucelon in nuclear fragmentation is a natural consequence of the transport theory, which predicts the formation of these structures around this beam energy.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the formation of bubbles and rings can be used to determine the time of the compression stage of nuclear collisions.
the nuclear equation of state can be probed by measuring the fragment multiplicities and the fragment velocities in the central collision of heavy ions.
the bubble and ring formation is not a mere geometrical artifact but is a consequence of the dynamics of the collision and can be observed in experiments.
